title: How a Leader Handles Criticism
subtitle: Every pastor will be criticized, and how a leader handles criticism in ministry reveals more about his heart than any sermon he will ever preach.

sections.title: Why It Cuts Deeper Than It Should
sections.body:
A man can preach to four hundred people who loved it and drive home thinking about the one who did not.

I have done it more times than I will admit. The note in the offering plate. The email that arrives Sunday night. The comment relayed by a friend who thought I should know. Ninety-nine kind words evaporate and the one cut stays, because criticism does not land on the work. It lands on the self, and the self in a leader is fused to the work in a way that makes every critique feel like a verdict on the soul.

This is the first thing to understand about criticism. It hurts out of all proportion because you have hidden your worth inside your work, and an attack on the work feels like an attack on your right to exist. That is not humility. That is a man who has made his ministry into his identity, and identity bleeds when it is struck.

The sting is information. It tells you where you have buried your soul.

sections.title: Learning to Tell the Critics Apart
sections.body:
Not all criticism is the same. Treating it as one thing is how leaders either crumble or grow hard, and both are deaths.

There is the faithful wound. A friend who loves you tells you a true and difficult thing, at cost to himself, because he would rather you hear it from him than fall. Proverbs calls these the wounds of a friend and says they are to be trusted. This critic is a gift wearing the disguise of pain, and a wise leader learns to thank him even while it stings.

There is the careless word. A tired person says a thoughtless thing on a hard day and means almost nothing by it. It is not a verdict. It is weather. You do not build a case against your ministry out of someone's bad Tuesday.

Then there is the malicious attack. A person with an agenda, a wound of his own, a hunger for control, who has decided you are the obstacle. This one is real and must be handled, but it must never be mistaken for the faithful wound, and the faithful wound must never be mistaken for it. The whole art is in the sorting. Most leaders never learn to sort. They take the friend's true word as an attack and the enemy's poison as gospel, exactly backward, and it ruins them.

sections.title: The Question to Ask Before You Defend
sections.body:
Before you answer any critic, ask one question. Is it true.

Not is it kind. Not is it fair. Not did he have the right to say it that way. Just this. Is there truth in it. Because a lie can come wrapped in cruelty and a truth can come wrapped in malice, and the wrapping is not the point. God has used the harshest, most unfair, most ill-motivated critic I ever had to show me a true thing I would not hear any other way. The man wanted to hurt me. God wanted to heal me. Both things happened in the same sentence.

This is the discipline that separates a formed leader from a defensive one. The defensive man hears criticism and immediately tries the speaker. Was he qualified. Was his tone right. Did he understand the context. And while he is busy prosecuting the messenger, the truth in the message walks past him untouched.

Sit with it before you answer. Take it to God before you take it to your defense. Ask Him to show you the one percent that is true even inside the ninety-nine that is not. That one percent is worth more than all your innocence on the other points.

sections.title: Where a Secure Leader Stands
sections.body:
You cannot handle criticism well from an empty soul. There is nothing to absorb it.

The leader who has no settled sense of God's love will treat every critic as a threat to his survival, because in a sense he is. If the approval of people is the ground you stand on, then every disapproval is an earthquake, and you will either fight to silence the critic or collapse to please him. Both are the behavior of a man standing on the wrong ground.

Paul wrote that it was a very small thing to him to be judged by anyone, that he did not even judge himself, that the one who judged him was the Lord. Read that and feel how free it is. Not arrogant. Free. He had moved his court of appeal. He no longer stood trial in the opinions of the Corinthians because he already stood, finally and forever, in the verdict of God over him in Christ. A man with that verdict secured can hear hard things without dying, because the worst has already been said about him and the blood has already answered it.

This is the only durable answer to criticism. Not thicker skin. A deeper standing. Get your worth settled in heaven and the earthly courtroom loses its power to destroy you.

sections.title: What to Actually Do With the Note
sections.body:
So here, plainly, is what to do when the criticism comes.

Do not answer fast. The reply written in the first hot hour is almost always the reply you will regret. Let it sit. Pray over it. Let the heat leave before the words do. Almost nothing in ministry must be answered today, and the things that feel most urgent are usually the things your pride is driving.

Find the friend who will tell you the truth about the criticism. Read it to someone who loves you and will neither flatter you nor pile on. Ask them, is there something here. They will see what your defensiveness hides.

Keep the true part and release the rest. Repent of what was real, thank God for showing you, and let the cruelty go without carrying it for ten years. Bitterness is just criticism you refused to either receive or release, left to rot inside you.

And bless the one who wounded you, even the malicious one, even the one who wanted to see you fall. Not because he deserves it. Because the alternative is to let him live rent-free in a soul that belongs to God. You answer to a higher court now. Act like a man who knows it.
